records.text: The course is called computer vision.
The course starts with deep learning basics.
Computer vision topics are pushed to the end of the course.
Over the last two weeks, a wide array of architectures and a set of tools to solve various problems were built up.
The architectures and tools are now being applied specifically to pictures.
Pictures have been discussed in the context of CNNs.
Pictures have not yet been discussed in the context of Transformers.
Alex explained the Vision Transformer (VIT) in practice sessions.
The main content of today's lecture is object detection.
Object detection is a problem in computer vision.
Object detection is one of the most interesting problems in computer vision.
Object detection is one of the hardest problems in computer vision.
Object detection has an unusual structure of outputs compared to segmentation.
Segmentation will not be discussed in lectures.
Alex might discuss segmentation in practice sessions.
Usually, a transformer replaces some part of an architecture and serves as a better feature extractor.
Often, there is nothing conceptually changing in the architecture when a transformer is used.
The UNET architecture is from approximately 2015.
Alex will tell about the UNET architecture.
Modern segmentation still uses UNET.
In modern segmentation, UNET uses self-attention based layers instead of convolutional layers.
The UNET did not become obsolete because the transformer appeared.
In object detection, the impact of transformers is different.
Visual Bird was one of the first successful approaches to handling pictures with transformers.
Visual Bird was mostly for captioning.
Visual Bird used text and object queries.
Object queries were tokens representing specific objects found on the picture.
To use Visual Bird, object detection had to be solved first.
Subsets of the image (rectangles) would be plugged into Visual Bird.
The rectangles correspond to specific objects on the input image.
The rectangles are passed through a simple embedding layer to get feature vectors.
The feature vectors are then processed by a transformer.
For a transformer, it matters little whether the input came from text, images, or other sources.
A transformer is great at finding internal correlations and structure within a sequence of vectors.
People straightforwardly applied transformers to images.
The most striking feature of the Vision Transformer (VIT) architecture is its simplicity.
The transformer architecture does not need to be changed when the input is an image.
When you cut a picture into patches, the patches do not naturally form a one-dimensional sequence.
In a fixed sequence of patches, adjacent patches in the sequence are not necessarily close on the image.
If you order patches row-first, the first three patches are neighbors.
After the third patch, the next patch goes to the left part of the image, and these two patches are far apart.
It is tempting to say that an image is not really a sequence.
An image has a two-dimensional structure.
To inform the transformer of the 2D structure, at least some change in positional encodings is needed.
For the transformer, the input is just a vector of features, but positions should be marked.
In the original VIT paper, an appendix shows that several ideas for positional encodings were tried and none helped.
Treating the patches as a sequence is sufficient.
Using standard positional encodings from text transformers works.
VIT revolutionized image processing and computer vision.
A transformer is better than previous methods.
VIT extracts better, more semantically rich features.
In many applications, replacing a convolutional network with VIT as the feature extractor, while keeping the rest of the architecture, yields better results.
After 2020, hundreds of papers replaced convolutional networks with VIT and kept the rest of the architecture.
The main computational problem of transformers is hard to solve.
VIT and any transformer have quadratic complexity.
In a transformer, the attention weight matrix is a token-by-token matrix of size L x L, where L is the input size.
It is hard to avoid the quadratic complexity.
VIT has complexity quadratic in the number of patches.
In VIT, every patch becomes a token at the input.
Given height h, width w, and patch size k x k, the number of patches is (h/k)*(w/k), and the complexity is squared of that number.
The grid size is squared in complexity.
In some applications, the quadratic complexity is a big problem.
You cannot have VIT go down to the level of individual pixels.
If the input has a million pixels, a million squared is too much computation.
Therefore, you have to use relatively big patches.
With relatively big patches, you cannot figure out small details of the image.
For object detection with VIT, if the object is small, it might be entirely inside one patch or on the boundary between patches, and none of the patches is dominated by this object.
If the object is small or on boundaries, it will be very hard for VIT because each patch is flattened to a single vector and details are lost.
There is no correct patch size for VIT.
If patches are too big, you lose detail; if patches are too small, the model is too heavy to train and run.
One approach to address the VIT patch size problem is the Swin Transformer.
The Swin Transformer is one of the most popular transformers for computer vision.
Today, many computer vision applications use VIT or Swin as the backbone.
Swin stands for shifted windows.
A natural way to reduce complexity is to break the image into parts and then cut each part into patches.
For example, with a 2x2 grid of parts, complexity in each part is the square of the number of patches in that part.
The summed complexity of the parts is much less than the original squared complexity.
Cutting the image into smaller pieces saves computation due to square complexity.
The complexity becomes effectively linear because the square is only over the small parts.

A hierarchical structure is natural: first cut the image into small parts (e.g., 4x4 grid), process each with VIT, combine and process with another VIT, then combine again and process globally with VIT.
In the hierarchical example, each transformer layer deals with only 16 tokens (4x4 grid parts).
In three steps, the 16x16 image is compressed to a 4x4 representation, then into features or a single vector.
When processing small parts of an image, having global context is often helpful.
For a small vehicle on a surface, it is hard to distinguish its exact type without context.
If the context is a highway, the vehicle is likely a car.
If the context is a sea lagoon, the vehicle is likely a boat.
Without global context, distinguishing between a car and a boat on a small patch is difficult.
Global context is often necessary in image understanding.
Small-patch processing should have access to information from the rest of the image.
In ShiftedWindows, between self-attention layers, the windows are shifted.
The picture from the SWIN transformer paper is a little bit misleading.
In the SWIN transformer, the first layer has a grid of patches.
In the next layer, the grid shifts by approximately half the patch size.
The transformer in the next layer is the same kind of transformer.
The transformer in the next layer still has the same input size.
The transformer in the next layer processes different subsets of features corresponding to different parts of the image.
If shifting is done after every layer, the receptive field of patches expands.
After multiple layers, a transformer in a higher layer sees a larger part of the image because it aggregates information from adjacent patches.
The picture shows the issues with the edges when shifting the grid.
Implementing the shifting grid has many edge-case issues that are easy to get wrong.
When the grid is shifted, patches near the edges do not form full squares.
Patches near the image edges become smaller, incomplete squares.
To handle edges, the image is wrapped onto a torus.
Patches that are split at edges are combined with patches from the opposite edge.
Rectangles from opposite edges and corners are combined together.
The edge handling is only relevant for edges, but it adds significant complexity.
There exists a 3D SWIN transformer implementation that uses cubes instead of squares.
That 3D SWIN transformer implementation was very convoluted.
It contained many hard-coded shifts and constants.
It was very difficult to understand.
The SWIN transformer and VIT can serve as good backbones.
A backbone is a part of a neural network that performs feature extraction.
A backbone is typically the largest part of the network.
By default, VIT is trained for classification.
VIT extracts features and collects them into a single vector at the end.
The single vector is used for reasoning about the image globally.
Today's topic is a different kind of application.
This application requires looking inside the image and mapping answers to specific pixels.
Mapping answers to specific pixels is more difficult than global classification.
The Perceiver architecture is skipped due to time constraints.
The main topic is object detection.
The first point was transformers for feature extraction from images.
The second point is object detection.
In object detection, an image may contain a cat and possibly other objects.
Object detection requires finding the cat in the image.
Object detection outputs the confidence (probability) that there is a cat.
Object detection outputs a rectangle around the cat.
The rectangle specifies the location of the cat.
The location is given as a rectangle, not pixel-level (which would be segmentation).
The rectangle is called a bounding box (abbreviated B box).
Object detection can handle multiple classes, such as cat and dog.
Object detection also aims to detect a dog and draw its bounding box.
Bounding boxes can overlap.
Objects can overlap.
Bounding box overlap can occur even if objects don't overlap, due to empty parts of rectangles.
For each detected object, the output must include a class label and a bounding box.
A bounding box is formalized by four numbers: x, y, width, height.
x and y represent the coordinates of a corner (e.g., bottom left).
Width and height specify the rectangle's dimensions.
A bounding box is defined by four numbers.
The input to an object detection neural network is the picture.
If an image contains only one object, the problem is object localization, which is easier.
The output must handle multiple objects.
For each object, a probability distribution over classes is output.
The probability distribution is like in classification.
For each object, the output includes four numbers for the bounding box (x, y, w, h).
A neural network cannot have a variable number of outputs.
The number of outputs must be fixed.
The number of outputs per object is: number of classes (for probabilities) plus four (for bounding box).
If the number of objects is known, the total outputs is determined.
The number of objects in an image is not known in advance; it can vary.
Output neurons have fixed weights, so variable outputs are not feasible.
The solution is to fix a maximal number of objects that can be detected.
The network has outputs for that maximal number of objects.
If there are fewer objects than the maximum, a way is needed to mark some outputs as not real.
For example, if the maximum is 10 but only 2 objects exist, 8 outputs are irrelevant.
The solution is to add a confidence output for each potential object.
The confidence is a probability between 0 and 1 indicating presence of an object.
If confidence is high, the corresponding class label and bounding box are considered valid.
For a correct prediction with two objects, the confidence should be 1 for those two and 0 for others.
Defining the output format is only the first step; a loss function is needed.
The ground truth consists of objects with known class and bounding box.
The loss function must handle unordered predictions.
The ground truth objects have no inherent ordering.
The network should not be forced to output objects in a specific order.
The goal is that the cat and dog appear in the output list with high confidence, and other outputs have low confidence.
A matching between ground truth objects and predictions is needed for the loss.
In object detection, the problem of assigning ground truth objects to predicted objects is referred to as an assignment problem.
The assignment problem requires pairing elements of two sets: the set of ground truth objects and the set of predicted objects.
One can pad the sets with a "no object" element up to a fixed count k.
The assignment aims to minimize some matching cost.
The Hungarian algorithm can be used to perform this assignment.
The Hungarian algorithm produces a bipartite matching between predictions and ground truth.
The matching produced by the Hungarian algorithm is one-to-one.
The assignment maps each ground truth box to the best matching predictor.
The loss function for training an object detector is composed of multiple parts.
One part is the confidence loss, which encourages the confidence score to be 1 if an object is present.
The confidence loss encourages the confidence score to be 0 if no object is present.
The confidence loss is often based on the logarithm of the confidence.
Another part is the classification loss.
The classification loss is applied only when an object is present.
When no object is present, the class label is ignored.
When an object is present, the classification loss is typically a cross-entropy between the predicted class distribution and the true class distribution.
The third part is the bounding box loss.
The bounding box loss measures the deviation of the predicted rectangle from the correct rectangle.
The bounding box loss is only considered when there is an object.
A simple form of bounding box loss is the sum of squared differences in coordinates, such as $(x - x_{\text{pred}})^2 + \ldots + (h - h_{\text{pred}})^2$.
Another simple form is the $L1$ loss, using absolute differences.
Coordinate-based losses like these have the problem that the loss contribution varies significantly between large and small objects.
For large objects, small coordinate errors can still result in significant overlap between boxes.
For small objects, identical coordinate errors can result in no overlap at all.
The original YOLO algorithm uses such a coordinate-based bounding box loss.
Modern object detection methods often use a loss based on Intersection over Union (IoU).
The IoU of two boxes is defined as the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union.
IoU is the default metric for evaluating the quality of a predicted bounding box against a ground truth box.
If two boxes do not overlap, their IoU is exactly 0.
IoU is differentiable.
Small changes to a bounding box produce small changes in IoU, enabling gradient-based optimization.
When the intersection area is zero, the gradient of IoU becomes uninformative (zero gradient).
When boxes are non-overlapping, moving a box in the right direction does not change the IoU (remains 0), so gradients cannot guide the movement.
Generalized IoU (GIoU) is an alternative metric that addresses the zero-gradient problem of IoU.
GIoU uses the concept of the smallest enclosing box that contains both boxes.
GIoU considers the proportion of the enclosing box not covered by the two boxes.
With GIoU, moving a box in the correct direction reduces the enclosing box size, providing a meaningful gradient.
Loss functions in object detection are independent of the specific neural network architecture.
As long as the architecture allows gradient passage, it can be used with the loss function.
Research on loss functions and architectures can proceed separately.
Even after optimal assignment between ground truth and predicted objects, one must determine which predictions correspond to actual objects.
A predicted box with sufficient overlap with a ground truth object should be matched to that object and have its confidence set to 1.
A predicted box with little overlap with any ground truth should have its confidence set to 0.
During training, a matching threshold based on IoU is used to decide positive matches.
If the IoU between a predicted box and a ground truth box exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.5), the prediction is considered a positive match.
If the IoU is below the threshold, the prediction is considered a negative match.
Object detectors produce a large number of predicted bounding boxes (up to a maximum possible number of objects).
In a typical image, only a small number of objects (e.g., two or three) are present.
Most predicted boxes should have their confidence pushed to 0.
An object detector may generate multiple overlapping bounding boxes for the same object.
Non-maximal suppression is a standard algorithm to select the best bounding box among multiple detections.
Non-maximal suppression is applied during inference, not training.
During inference, non-maximal suppression combines multiple detection hypotheses into a single box per object.
The lecture does not go back in history before deep learning.
The course is on deep learning.
The lecture goes back 10 years to 2014.
After AlexNet revolutionized image processing, people tried to apply deep learning everywhere for images.
Eventually, deep learning was applied to object detection.
The first successful attempt at deep learning-based object detection was called RCNN.
RCNN stands for region-based CNN.
Ross Gershuk is one of the best known researchers in object detection.
The original RCNN approach used an external algorithm called selective search to produce candidate bounding boxes.
The selective search algorithm does not know the classes.
Selective search just finds distinctive objects on the photo.
Selective search produces hundreds of candidate bounding boxes, of which only a few are actual objects.
In RCNN, every candidate bounding box is passed through a neural network (a CNN trained on ImageNet) separately.
This CNN is called the backbone.
The CNN outputs the class of object in the bounding box.
To put a bounding box through a CNN pre-trained on ImageNet, the box must be square because the CNN expects a 256x256 square input.
In RCNN, bounding boxes were warped (artificially geometrically compressed) to become square.
This warping actually worked.
A CNN trained on ImageNet presumes there is an object in the input and only classifies it; it does not tell whether there is an object or not.
If given a bad bounding box (e.g., sky with clouds), the CNN outputs a distribution over classes with no confidence.
RCNN had a third step: a model on top of the CNN outputs that further classifies based on the probabilities whether it is a real object or not.
The RCNN approach was very fragile.
The RCNN approach was the best approach at the time.
RCNN was hopelessly slow: about one minute per image on a GPU.
All the ideas of two-stage object detection are already in the original RCNN architecture.
The speaker used to have very detailed lectures on object detection covering dozens of different architectures, but will not do that due to time and decreasing relevance.
The RCNN family is still relevant because it explains the main ideas of two-stage object detection.
The main idea in basic RCNN is to use a backbone to extract features from a specific part of the input.
In basic RCNN, candidate bounding boxes come from an external algorithm; later they come from the network itself.
Two-stage object detection first produces a relatively small set of candidate bounding boxes, then processes each bounding box.
Processing every bounding box independently in RCNN is hopelessly slow.
To get good coverage of actual objects in RCNN, 2,000 region proposals are needed.
The 47 seconds of processing time per image in RCNN come from running the same network 2,000 times and then running a model on top.
The next step was an approach called faster CNN, which introduced the idea to process the whole image only once.
In faster CNN, features are extracted from the feature tensor by taking parts of the feature tensor, rather than reprocessing from pixels each time.
In faster CNN, the image is passed through the CNN only once, stopping a bit short to get a feature tensor that still has geometry.
In faster CNN, candidate bounding boxes are still produced by an external algorithm.
Candidate bounding boxes can be projected onto the feature tensor by ROI projection because there is a correspondence between features and pixels.
ROI stands for region of interest.
ROI projection is not trainable; it is based on which features look at which pixels.
The projected bounding box inside the feature tensor is then passed through an object detection head that has a classifier and a bounding box regressor.
Bounding box regression is always used, even when candidates are already in pixels, because the network may want to shift the box slightly and this can be trained.
In faster CNN, the big convolutional network is run only once, and for each bounding box only the small detection head is run, making it orders of magnitude faster.
A technical problem in faster CNN is that bounding boxes map to parts of the feature tensor of different sizes, but the detection head requires fixed-size input.
The solution to this problem is a region of interest pooling layer.
ROI pooling works by dividing the bounding box region in the feature tensor into a fixed number of bins (e.g., 2x2) and pooling within each bin.
ROI pooling is used everywhere starting from faster CNN.
The faster CNN approach was orders of magnitude faster, and the remaining bottleneck was the external algorithm producing candidate boxes.
The next iteration was faster RCNN, which still counts as two-stage detection.
In faster RCNN, proposals are produced by a separate part of the network: the region proposal network (RPN) inside the architecture.
The RPN works on the same feature map and uses a sliding window to find which boxes make sense.
The RPN outputs a few top boxes (maybe hundreds).
After RPN, the rest of the pipeline is the same: ROI pooling, detection head, etc.
Faster RCNN became the standard approach for object detection until Transformers changed everything.
Transformers changed everything not in 2017, but much later after ViT and everything.
For quite a few years, faster RCNN was the standard way to do object detection when you have time.
Two-stage detection is pretty slow.
Object detection shines when using a very smart, very complicated backbone (a good network).
Convolutional Neural Networks progressed from VGGs to ResNets to EfficientNets.
In an object detection meta-architecture, you can plug in a different backbone without changing other components.
Using a better backbone yields a better object detector.
The discussion has shifted from specific architectures to meta-architectures.
A meta-architecture consists of a neural network that extracts features, performs region proposal, and other stages.
The top parts (heads) of the meta-architecture are more or less fixed.
The bottom part (backbone) of the meta-architecture can be substituted with any feature extractor.
Whenever a new and better feature extractor is developed, it improves object detection for free.
This has always been the case in object detection development.
One-stage object detection is a separate line of work where detection is performed in a single network pass.
In one-stage detection, there is no separate stage for proposals, unlike two-stage detection.
In two-stage detectors, a stage generates proposals, ranks them, selects top proposals, and applies heavy processing to them.
In one-stage detection, the network evaluates many candidate proposals in a single pass.
Going over all possible rectangles pixel-wise inside an image is computationally too expensive (on the order of the number of pixels squared).
One-stage detectors instead consider reasonable bounding box candidates at some level of granularity.
The YOLO family best exemplifies one-stage object detection.
The YOLO family uses a single neural architecture that processes the image.
The YOLO architecture evaluates many candidates in parallel and outputs results for all candidates.
The outputs from YOLO can be ranked to select the top detections as needed.
There was the original YOLO detector.
Then YOLO v2 was developed.
YOLO 9000 was a version with many classes and used hierarchical softmax.
Then YOLO v3 was developed.
As YOLO architectures evolved, they changed through many small modifications.
There is rarely a single big idea that constitutes a major leap in these architectures.
Improvements typically come from about 10 small tweaks.
Each individual tweak provides roughly a 2% increase in accuracy on the evaluated metric.
Combining all these tweaks results in about a 15% overall improvement, which is a huge leap forward.
Detecting small objects is the main problem in object detection, both classical and contemporary.
Detecting small objects is the hardest part and sometimes impossible.
If an object takes up about a quarter of the image, most object detection algorithms will recognize it fine.
This is true starting from original Faster R-CNN and YOLO v2.
Detecting a small object in the distance presents a crucial trade-off or dilemma that cannot be fully resolved.
This dilemma involves choosing a level of granularity in the feature extraction.
In Faster R-CNN, you process the image through a CNN to extract features and must decide at which layer to stop.
Stopping too late in the CNN results in loss of geometric information, leading to a coarse feature grid.
A small object may fall entirely within one feature vector and thus its information is lost, making it unrecognizable.
Stopping too early yields a fine grid enabling small object recognition.
Processing on a too fine grid is infeasible because it requires considering many candidate bounding boxes.
It is infeasible to perform detection directly on a very fine grid, similar to pixel-level processing.
Looking for only small objects on a fine grid becomes feasible and eliminates the quadratic complexity.
Multi-stage object detection uses different stages of the CNN at different scales: early layers for small objects, later layers for medium and large objects.
This multi-scale detection allows detection at three scales (small, medium, large).
Multi-scale detection is more expensive than single-scale but not prohibitively so.
When recognizing small objects, having global context is very helpful.
Small objects are hard to recognize because they consist of only a few pixels.
Humans also struggle to recognize objects from a few-pixel crop without the whole image context.
The Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) was a very fruitful idea developed after Faster R-CNN.
FPN uses a bottom-up path for large objects, and fuses features from more global scales for detecting medium and small objects.
FPN adds only a couple of extra layers for fusion, not increasing workload significantly.
FPN allows the network to capture global context, making it very influential.
Many variations and improvements were made based on FPN and multi-scale detection.
The EfficientNet family uses neural architecture search to find efficient CNN architectures.
There is a parallel line of work that searches for the optimal post-processing architecture using a fixed EfficientNet backbone.
In post-processing, one can experiment with different connections (e.g., up/down paths, skip layers) at relatively low cost.
Such experimentation led to further advances in object detection.
The preceding methods constitute 'classical' object detection within deep learning, though the term 'classical' usually refers to pre-deep learning methods.
Transformers appeared, and the Vision Transformer (ViT) happened.
This raised the question of how transformers could be applied to object detection and whether they could simplify it.
Transformers taught that in deep learning, one can often use a single excellent architecture (like the transformer) to handle everything without specialized components.
It turns out transformers can be used for object detection, leading to interesting approaches.
The first architecture in this direction was DETR (Detection Transformer).
DETR still uses a CNN backbone to extract image features; the Transformer is not used for feature extraction from the raw image.
The CNN backbone outputs a set of image features.
Positional encodings are added to these features.
The resulting sequence of vectors is fed into a Transformer encoder.
The Transformer encoder does not perform detection; it simply processes the features by mixing them together.
The backbone is trained together with the rest of the model to produce features suitable for object detection.
The interesting part of the architecture occurs in the decoder.
The architecture is a full-scale transformer.
The architecture is not BERT.
The architecture is not GPT.
The architecture is an encoder-decoder architecture.
In the transformer decoder, there is an encoder-decoder attention mechanism.
In the encoder-decoder attention, the queries come from the decoder.
For a language model, the queries come from the prefix that the decoder has already written.
In the encoder-decoder attention, the keys and values come from the encoder.
The keys and values come from the vectors produced by the encoder.
In DETR, there is no autoregressive generation.
In DETR, there is a set of object queries.
Object queries can be vectors that are trained together with the rest of the model.
Alternatively, object queries can be fixed random vectors.
Object queries are passed through the decoder layers.
Cross-attention from the encoder informs the object queries during decoding.
The information in the decoder comes from the encoder.
The image information comes from the encoder.
Each output vector from the decoder is used as input to the detection head.
The detection head is a small feed-forward network.
The detection head performs confidence classification.
The detection head performs bounding box regression.
The input to the detection head is the transformed object query vector.
The number of recognized objects equals the number of object queries.
The number of object queries must be fixed in advance.
The number of object queries does not change during inference.
A backbone network maps the input image to features.
The feature grid from the backbone is flattened into a set of vectors.
The original feature grid had a width and height.
The spatial dimensions of the feature grid are discarded after flattening.
The flattened image features are turned into a set of vectors.
Positional encodings are added to the feature vectors.
The feature vectors with positional encodings are processed by the encoder-decoder transformer architecture.
An object query acts as a slot for a possible object.
In DETR, object queries tend to specialize.
Object queries may specialize for small objects in the middle of the image.
Object queries may specialize for large objects on the left side of the image.
Object queries probably do not specialize by class.
Object queries specialize by location.
Most object queries predict no object.
Most object queries drive the confidence score to zero.
A large number of object queries (e.g., 100) are used.
Images typically contain far fewer objects than the number of queries.
In DETR, non-maximal suppression is not needed.
The reason non-maximal suppression is not needed is that the object queries exchange information with each other.
Object queries exchange information in the transformer decoder.
Through information exchange, object queries further specialize.
In DETR output, there is not a large number of nearly identical bounding boxes around a single object (e.g., a seagull).
There will typically be just one bounding box per object.
Object queries learn to not duplicate detections.
DETR has a problem with scale.
DETR operates on a single scale.
In DETR, an image is passed through a backbone CNN to produce features.
The architecture cannot recover small objects lost during feature extraction.
Small objects are lost in the process.
Detection performance for small objects is likely poor.
You can visualize the attention heads in the decoder.
The self-attention in the decoder shows that object queries become very specialized for objects.
The next modification to address the scale problem is called Deformable DETR.
Deformable DETR can operate at multiple scales.
Deformable DETR addresses the scale problem by processing different scales separately for small and large objects.
Deformable DETR uses deformable attention.
In DETR, the attention weights focus on pixels at object boundaries.
Decoder attention is localized on object boundaries.
In DETR, once the decoder attention is localized on boundaries, the objects are already separated.
After attention separates objects, the remaining task is to classify them and refine the bounding box.
Attention in different heads separates the objects.
The transformer has quadratic complexity, which prevents it from working on fine grids.
To avoid quadratic complexity, attention can be restricted to a small subset of feature vectors.
The subset of feature vectors to attend to is not known in advance.
In deformable attention, each attention head looks at several positions on the image and collects features from those positions.
The locations of the positions to attend to are learned during training.
Using deformable attention, it becomes feasible to use a multi-scale feature map in the transformer.
In a standard transformer, multi-scale features would require attending to every token, leading to high complexity.
A fine grid results in quadratic complexity, which is computationally prohibitive.
Deformable DETR deals with quadratic complexity by restricting attention to a small subset of input tokens.
Another set of ideas focuses on improving the object queries.
The bounding boxes predicted by object queries tend to be distributed across the input image.
Learning to specialize object queries is slow and unstable.
One idea is to initialize object queries from a grid or random points to improve them.
Dynamic Anchor Box DETR (DAB-DETR) uses object queries that are bounding boxes (anchors) rather than abstract vectors.
In DAB-DETR, object queries are bounding boxes with parameters x, y, h, w.
In DAB-DETR, object queries can be initialized in a way that they are already spatially separate from the start.
The bounding box representation provides clear semantics, allowing for smarter refinement across layers.
DAB-DETR achieves better object queries (anchors) in less training time.
The best current object detectors include DINO and its modifications, as well as Deformable DETR.
All transformer-based object detectors share the basic idea from original DETR that object queries (bounding boxes) are queries to a transformer decoder.
The transformer decoder fills these queries with content based on the image.
